reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / Endocrine Society clinical guidance
clinicalPearls: Defined by the presence of both ovarian tissue (with follicles) and testicular tissue (with seminiferous tubules) in the same individual, either as separate gonads or combined in an ovotestis
The most common karyotype is 46,XX, with 46,XX/46,XY chimerism and 46,XY seen less often
External genitalia are usually ambiguous, and the degree of virilisation reflects the amount and function of the testicular component
Mullerian and wolffian structures may coexist, with a uterus often present on the side bearing ovarian tissue
Definitive diagnosis requires gonadal histology demonstrating both tissue types, not imaging alone
Management is individualised around sex of rearing, functional gonadal potential and malignancy risk, with retention of gonadal tissue matched to the assigned sex where feasible
Gonadal tissue containing Y material or dysgenetic elements carries tumour risk and warrants removal or close surveillance
reference.pathophysiology: Ovotesticular disorder of sex development arises when the bipotential gonad differentiates into both ovarian and testicular tissue within the same person. In 46,XX cases this can follow cryptic or translocated SRY, gain-of-function in the testis-promoting pathway (for example SOX9 duplication) or as-yet-undefined mechanisms that allow partial testis determination without a Y chromosome. The mixed gonadal tissue secretes a variable combination of testosterone and anti-mullerian hormone, so internal ducts and external genitalia develop along an intermediate path determined locally by the dominant tissue on each side. The result is a spectrum of ambiguity, and gonadal segments with testicular or dysgenetic elements can predispose to germ cell tumours.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia causing virilisation of a 46,XX infant
additionalInvestigations: Karyotype and molecular studies including SRY and copy-number analysis for SOX9
Pelvic and gonadal imaging by ultrasound or MRI to localise gonads and mullerian structures
Serum testosterone, anti-mullerian hormone and gonadotropins, with hCG stimulation to assess testicular function
Gonadal biopsy and histopathology to confirm the presence of both tissue types
Adrenal steroid profiling (including 17-hydroxyprogesterone) to exclude congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Germ cell tumour surveillance of retained gonadal tissue
redFlags: Ambiguous genitalia in a newborn requiring urgent exclusion of salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia
An enlarging gonadal mass suggesting germ cell malignancy in dysgenetic or Y-bearing tissue
Progressive inappropriate virilisation or feminisation after sex assignment
Delayed or absent puberty indicating gonadal insufficiency
reference.prognosis: Outcomes depend on gonadal function preserved after surgery, the assigned sex and psychosocial support; fertility has occasionally been reported, particularly from the ovarian component. Malignancy risk in retained testicular or dysgenetic tissue necessitates lifelong awareness and surveillance.
pitfalls: Assuming imaging can distinguish ovotestis from other gonads without histology
Overlooking coexisting congenital adrenal hyperplasia as a cause of ambiguity
Removing potentially functional gonadal tissue congruent with the sex of rearing
Neglecting the malignancy risk of retained Y-bearing or dysgenetic components
references: Endocrine Society clinical practice guidance on disorders of sex development
management: Manage within a specialist multidisciplinary disorders-of-sex-development team, individualising decisions around sex of rearing, gonadal function and malignancy risk
Undertake gonadal surgery matched to the assigned sex, removing discordant or dysgenetic gonadal tissue while retaining functional tissue where feasible
Provide sex-steroid hormone replacement, oestrogen or testosterone, to induce and maintain puberty and secondary sexual characteristics appropriate to the assigned sex
Offer genital reconstructive surgery where indicated, timed and planned with the family and the young person
Maintain germ cell tumour surveillance of any retained testicular or dysgenetic gonadal tissue, or perform gonadectomy where malignancy risk is high
Provide psychological support to the child or young person and family throughout
Offer genetic counselling with karyotype and molecular characterisation including SRY and SOX9 to inform diagnosis and recurrence risk
